beats.say: Mercury. The silver liquid in old thermometers. In October twenty twenty six, a startup said it had turned it into real gold.
Alchemists failed at this for nearly two thousand years. So how?
Gold is rare, and it never rusts. Every bit ever mined would fit in one cube, about twenty two metres across.
For centuries, people tried to make it. Even Isaac Newton.
Chemistry can't turn one metal into another.
That takes breaking into the atom, which Ernest Rutherford first did in nineteen nineteen.
In nineteen forty one, Harvard scientists hit mercury with neutrons, and got a few atoms of radioactive gold.
In twenty twenty five, the Large Hadron Collider team showed it makes specks of gold from lead, gone in a split second.
The secret? Every element is a number: the protons in the centre of its atoms.
Gold is seventy nine. Mercury is eighty. Next-door neighbours.
Fusion fires fast neutrons into mercury. Each hit knocks a neutron out, and the atom turns unstable.
Within days, a proton turns into a neutron. Eighty becomes seventy nine. Mercury becomes gold.
The catch: some of the fresh gold is radioactive. The company's own paper says it must wait almost eighteen years to be less radioactive than a banana.
Marathon says it beat CERN's gold record by ten times. It hasn't said how much gold, and no one else has checked yet.
A big fusion plant might make a few tonnes a year. And no fusion plant sells power yet.
Newton chased gold with a furnace. Now someone says they've made it with fusion. If gold can be made, would it still feel like gold?
